pharm: Low molecular weight heparin obtained by depolymerization of standard heparin; acts as an anticoagulant mainly through antithrombin-mediated inhibition of factor Xa (with relatively less anti-IIa/thrombin activity).
quick: VTE prophylaxis: 3,200-4,250 anti-Xa IU SC once daily; treatment: ~6,400 IU SC once daily (per regional SmPC)
Subcutaneous injection; not related to meals
Use only if clearly needed; LMWHs do not cross placenta but use under specialist guidance; avoid multidose vials with benzyl alcohol
Minimal oral absorption by infant; generally considered compatible
Caution and dose reduction in severe renal impairment (accumulation/bleeding risk); monitor anti-Xa
Limit; heavy use raises bleeding/GI risk
Platelets (HIT), signs of bleeding, renal function; anti-Xa if monitoring needed
summary: Parnaparin is a low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) produced by controlled depolymerization of unfractionated heparin. Like other LMWHs, it binds antithrombin and accelerates inhibition of activated coagulation factors, predominantly factor Xa, with comparatively less anti-thrombin (anti-IIa) activity, giving a more predictable anticoagulant response and a longer half-life than unfractionated heparin. It is used for prophylaxis and treatment of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), prevention of clotting in extracorporeal circuits, and treatment of superficial venous thrombophlebitis, given by subcutaneous injection (anti-Xa IU dosing). It is NOT approved by the US FDA and is marketed in Europe and other regions (e.g., Fluxum); dosing follows the regional summary of product characteristics. Key risks are bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT); platelet counts and signs of bleeding should be monitored, and dose adjusted in renal impairment. Like other LMWHs, it carries the spinal/epidural hematoma concern when neuraxial anesthesia or puncture is used.
indications: Prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism in surgical and high-risk medical patients
Treatment of established deep vein thrombosis (and venous thromboembolic disease)
Prevention of clotting in the extracorporeal circuit during hemodialysis
Treatment of superficial venous thrombophlebitis (per regional labeling)

dosage.n: Start perioperatively per protocol; continue for the at-risk period (per SmPC)

dosage.d: Approximately 6,400 anti-Xa IU subcutaneously once daily (treatment-dose regimen per SmPC)
dosage.t: Once daily for the treatment course
dosage.n: Overlap with oral anticoagulant as indicated; adjust per renal function

admin: Administer by deep subcutaneous injection, typically into the anterolateral or posterolateral abdominal wall; alternate sides
Do not give by intramuscular injection
Do not expel the air bubble from prefilled syringes before injecting; do not rub the site afterward
Use anti-Xa IU dosing units; do not interchange unit-for-unit with other heparins or LMWHs
Not FDA-approved - follow the regional (EU/SmPC) product information; observe neuraxial anesthesia precautions
moa: Parnaparin is a low molecular weight heparin formed by depolymerization of unfractionated heparin to fragments with a mean molecular weight of roughly 4,000-6,000 daltons. It exerts its anticoagulant effect by binding to and potentiating antithrombin (antithrombin III); the heparin-antithrombin complex inactivates activated clotting factors. Because of its shorter chain length, it preferentially accelerates inhibition of factor Xa relative to thrombin (factor IIa), giving a higher anti-Xa to anti-IIa activity ratio than standard heparin. This produces effective anticoagulation with a more predictable dose-response, higher subcutaneous bioavailability, and a longer half-life, allowing once-daily fixed/weight-based dosing without routine coagulation monitoring in most patients.

absolute: Active major bleeding or bleeding disorders / hemorrhagic diathesis
Known hypersensitivity to parnaparin, heparin, or pork products
Acute bacterial endocarditis; recent hemorrhagic stroke; active peptic ulcer with bleeding
relative: Severe renal impairment (accumulation - reduce dose / monitor)
Severe hepatic impairment, uncontrolled severe hypertension
Recent neurosurgery/ophthalmic surgery, neuraxial (spinal/epidural) anesthesia or puncture (hematoma risk)
monitor: Renal function (and anti-Xa levels where indicated)
Serum potassium (heparins can cause hyperkalemia via aldosterone suppression)

preg: Low molecular weight heparins do not cross the placenta. Parnaparin may be used in pregnancy when clearly indicated, under specialist supervision; avoid multidose presentations containing benzyl alcohol during pregnancy. Use the lowest effective dose and monitor as appropriate. (Based on regional SmPC; the drug is not FDA-approved.)
lact: Low molecular weight heparins are large molecules that pass poorly into breast milk and would be degraded in the infant's gastrointestinal tract, so significant absorption by a breastfed infant is not expected. Breastfeeding is generally considered compatible. (Based on regional SmPC and LMWH class data.)
renal: Parnaparin is partly cleared renally and can accumulate in renal impairment, increasing bleeding risk. Use with caution and reduce the dose in severe renal impairment; consider anti-factor Xa monitoring to guide therapy. (Per regional SmPC.)
hepatic: Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment because of altered coagulation and increased bleeding risk; monitor for bleeding. No standardized dose-adjustment scheme is specified.

major: Other anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs, unfractionated heparin), thrombolytics - markedly increased bleeding risk
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs, dipyridamole) - increased bleeding risk
moderate: Drugs causing hyperkalemia (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements) - additive hyperkalemia
Systemic corticosteroids - increased risk of bleeding/gastric ulceration
minor: Drugs that affect platelet function or gastric mucosa may add to bleeding tendency
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; heavy or chronic use increases gastrointestinal and bleeding risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor platelet count for HIT; anti-factor Xa activity (not aPTT) is used when laboratory monitoring is required; LMWHs may transiently elevate liver transaminases.

common: Asymptomatic, reversible elevation of liver transaminases
serious: Spinal or epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia/puncture (may cause paralysis)
rare: Hypersensitivity / allergic reactions, skin necrosis at injection site
emergency: Spinal/epidural hematoma (back pain, leg weakness, numbness, bladder/bowel dysfunction)

monitoring: Platelet count before and periodically during therapy to detect heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Signs and symptoms of bleeding and hemoglobin/hematocrit
Renal function, especially in the elderly and at-risk patients; anti-factor Xa levels where monitoring is indicated
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hyperkalemia
Neurologic status if neuraxial anesthesia/puncture has been used (spinal hematoma)
counsel: This is a blood thinner given by injection under the skin to prevent or treat blood clots
Watch for and report unusual bleeding or bruising, blood in urine or stool, black stools, nosebleeds, or coughing up blood
Learn proper injection technique and rotate sites; do not push out the air bubble in prefilled syringes and do not rub the site afterward
Tell all your doctors and dentists that you are on this medicine, and avoid aspirin/NSAIDs unless approved
Seek urgent care for severe back pain, leg weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder/bowel control, especially after a spinal procedure
pk: Anticoagulant (anti-Xa) effect within a few hours of subcutaneous injection
Peak anti-factor Xa activity approximately 3-4 hours after subcutaneous dosing
Anti-Xa elimination half-life approximately 6 hours (longer than unfractionated heparin)
Anticoagulant effect over ~24 hours, supporting once-daily dosing
Store below 25-30 C (do not freeze); keep prefilled syringes in the original packaging until use
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - marketed in Europe and other regions (e.g., Fluxum); dosing follows the regional SmPC and is expressed in anti-Xa IU
Dose units are NOT interchangeable with unfractionated heparin or other LMWHs - never substitute unit-for-unit
Monitor platelets for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT); contraindicated with a history of immune HIT
Observe strict neuraxial anesthesia precautions - spinal/epidural hematoma can cause permanent paralysis; time procedures around dosing
Reduce dose and monitor in renal impairment; protamine only partially reverses LMWH anti-Xa activity
missed: If a once-daily dose is missed, inject it as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular once-daily schedule - do not give a double dose. Contact the prescriber if unsure.
overdose: Overdose mainly manifests as bleeding. Discontinue the drug. Protamine sulfate partially neutralizes the anti-factor Xa activity of low molecular weight heparins (roughly neutralizing the anti-IIa effect but only partially the anti-Xa effect); it can be given to control significant hemorrhage, with the dose based on the amount and timing of parnaparin administered. Provide supportive care, including transfusion of blood products as needed, and monitor coagulation parameters.
